questions.question: A shoe manufacturer wants to sell shoes and buy wheat. In a barter system without money, what difficulty does he immediately encounter?
options: He must obtain an export license from the United Nations
He must find a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat, but also wants to buy the exact size and style of shoes he makes
He is legally prohibited from consuming wheat products
He can only trade with merchants who speak foreign languages
questions.explanation: Both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. If the farmer wants clothes instead of shoes, no exchange can occur — the classic obstacle of double coincidence of wants.

questions.question: What would happen to a commercial bank if all of its depositors arrive on the exact same morning demanding to withdraw their entire savings in cash?
options: The bank would immediately double its profits by collecting withdrawal fees
The bank would print new paper currency in its back office within ten minutes
The bank would face a liquidity crisis ('bank run') and be unable to pay all depositors immediately because most funds are tied up in long-term loans
The bank manager would be declared the permanent governor of the Reserve Bank
questions.explanation: Because banks keep only about 15% cash reserves based on the statistical assumption that not all depositors withdraw money on the same day, a simultaneous mass withdrawal causes a run on the bank.

questions.question: What is meant by the economic term 'debt-trap'?
options: A government tax audit conducted on private commercial companies
An automated machine that detects counterfeit currency notes
A legal contract restricting a worker from changing employers
A situation where credit pushes the borrower into a financial crisis from which recovery is impossible without selling productive assets or taking further debt
questions.explanation: A debt-trap occurs when repayment of a loan requires taking another loan or selling productive assets (like land). Instead of improving the borrower's earnings, credit leaves them worse off and trapped in compounding debt.

questions.subtopic: Agricultural Trader as Lender: Tied Credit
questions.question: In the NCERT fieldwork in Sonpur village, farmer Arun borrows from a trader at the beginning of the cropping season. In exchange for the loan, the trader extracts which restrictive condition?
options: The farmer promises to sell his entire paddy crop to the trader at a pre-fixed price lower than prevailing market rates
The farmer agrees to surrender his voting rights in general elections
The farmer must work as an unpaid domestic servant for five years
The farmer promises to give 90% of his land to the trader's children
questions.explanation: Traders often provide loans on the condition that farmers sell their crop to them. This ensures the trader recovers the loan money and also buys crop at a low price, making huge profits by reselling it later at high market rates.

questions.subtopic: Cheap Credit as an Engine for National Development
questions.question: Why is the availability of 'cheap and affordable formal credit' considered crucial for a country's economic development?
options: It eliminates the need for citizens to work or produce goods
It forces commercial banks to forgive all international foreign debts
It replaces all income taxes with private bank loans
It allows enterprises and small farmers to borrow, invest, establish new manufacturing units, expand output, and generate incomes without falling into debt traps
questions.explanation: Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development. High cost of borrowing means a large part of earnings is spent to repay the loan, leaving little for investment. Affordable credit promotes new businesses, agricultural investments, and employment.

Expand overall formal lending in rural areas and ensure that formal credit is distributed more equally so that the poor can benefit from cheaper loans

questions.question: Why does the RBI mandate that commercial banks allocate a minimum percentage of their net bank credit to the 'Priority Sector' (agriculture, micro-enterprises, education)?

To convert private commercial banks into non-profit religious trusts
To prevent banks from lending exclusively to large urban corporate conglomerates and ensure that vulnerable, employment-generating sectors receive necessary credit
To eliminate interest payments on all urban housing loans
questions.explanation: Left to market forces alone, banks would lend only to large, safe, profit-maximizing urban corporations. RBI rules ensure credit flows to agriculture and small enterprises vital for national livelihood.
